title: AI consulting services: is it worth it, and what does it cost?
description: When outside AI help pays, what you should walk away with, and what it costs against hiring your own AI team. For COOs and heads of operations.
job: deciding whether to hire outside AI help
verdict: Hire help for one workflow with a business number attached, not a strategy deck.[^3][^2]
Partnered projects reached deployment about twice as often in MIT's sample, and most enterprise AI is now bought.[^1][^15]
Walk away with a before number, a pilot in daily use and a plan your team runs.[^5][^1]
Your people keep the decisions: most firms using AI use it only to help staff.[^7][^4]
Start with a free 30-minute diagnostic or a no-cost SBDC advisor before you pay anyone.[^17][^13]

onPage.text: The five things good AI help should leave you holding
Who on your team keeps each decision
Three shapes the work can take, and what each costs
What it costs to hire an AI team yourself, from US pay data
Why most AI pilots stall, and the fix for each
Twelve checks to judge any AI advisor before you sign

summary: AI consulting is outside help to pick one workflow, prove AI on your own work and get it into daily use.[^3][^1] What changes: your team runs AI on that work every day, measured against a before number.[^5][^4] Partnered projects reached daily use about twice as often as internal builds.[^1]
walkAway: One workflow, picked from a ranked list, with a named owner and the business number it should move.[^3] RAND's most common cause of AI failure is a misunderstood problem or the wrong metric.[^2]
A before number, measured before any tool is bought: volume, hours, errors or cost per item.[^5]
A pilot running in daily work, not a demo. In MIT's interviews, only 5% of custom enterprise AI tools reached production.[^1]
A plan your own team can run, with named owners and training.[^4] Most small-business owners, 73%, say more training would help them put AI to work.[^11]
Everything handed over as files you keep: test cases, answer key, specs and code.[^17] Then you can re-run the test when a cheaper model ships.[^27]
humanRole: COO or head of operations: owns the go, change or stop call, and the AI risk that comes with it. NIST, the US standards agency, puts AI risk decisions with executive leadership.[^4]

Process owner (ops lead, plant manager, claims or service lead): picks the workflow, agrees the right answers and checks AI output.[^4][^3] MIT found the strongest projects were sourced from frontline managers.[^1]
A named reviewer approves anything that moves money or reaches customers, such as refunds or payments, until the system earns trust.[^10] Your firm stays liable for what its AI tells customers.[^9]
The advisor builds, tests and coaches; your staff run the work.[^4] Among US firms using AI, 66% use it only to help staff with tasks, and AI-related employment fell at 2%.[^7]

recipes.name: 1. Free first pass: one workflow, no fee
recipes.when: Pick this when you have one idea, no data team and no budget yet. Small Business Development Centers (SBDCs) give no-cost advice; Manufacturing Extension Partnership (MEP) centers serve manufacturers.[^13][^14]
flow: COO: name the three jobs that cost the most time or errors
Ops lead: time one of them for two weeks to get a before number
Advisor: in a 30-minute call, say buy, build or skip, and what to test first
COO: pick one job and set a go-or-stop date
recipes.cost: Free. Our diagnostic is 30 minutes, and SBDC advice is no-cost.[^17][^13]

recipes.name: 2. Fixed-scope sprint: rank and spec the first bets
recipes.when: Pick this when several teams want AI and you need a ranked list your board or lender will back. Ask any advisor for a fixed scope and a price agreed up front.
flow: COO: sponsor it and name an owner for each candidate workflow
Division heads: bring their two costliest jobs and today's numbers
Advisor: score each job on value, data, risk and owner
Your team: agree the right answers on 50 real cases, then lock them
Advisor: test the leading options on those cases
COO: approve the 90-day plan, with owners and what not to do
recipes.cost: One fixed fee for 30 days, agreed before work starts.[^17] You get 2 or 3 ranked bets, specs your team or a vendor can build from, and a 90-day plan.[^17]

recipes.name: 3. Advisory while your team or a vendor builds
recipes.when: Pick this when the first workflow is chosen and a build is under way. Running the model is at least 70% of its lifetime cost, so someone must keep checking it.[^24]
flow: Process owner: run the build with your own team or a vendor
Named reviewer: clear the queue of cases the AI is unsure about
IT lead: log every AI decision and who checked it
Process owner: go live at one site or team first, then scale
Advisor: review progress twice a month and flag new models or prices
Advisor: re-run the locked test when a cheaper model ships
COO: go, change or stop at each quarter
recipes.cost: A monthly fee, with a quarterly commitment.[^17] The build itself is quoted per job, or done by your team or a vendor from the specs.[^17]

ownData.title: What does it cost to hire an AI team yourself?
ownData.intro: A lean in-house AI team of one manager, one data scientist and one developer costs about $630,000 a year with benefits, by our math.[^19][^18][^20][^21] The figures are US median pay from the Bureau of Labor Statistics for May 2025. AI job titles have no BLS group of their own, so each row uses the nearest one.
rows: Computer and information systems manager, nearest to a head of AI
Computer and information research scientist, nearest to a machine learning engineer
Software developer, nearest to an AI engineer
ownData.note: Source: BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook, May 2025 median pay, checked 26 November 2026.[^19][^22][^20][^18] Cost with benefits divides median pay by 68.5%, the wage share of pay costs for full-time private workers in June 2026.[^21] Medians cover all employers and experience levels, and filling each role takes time too.[^23]

watchOuts: Wrong problem or wrong metric: RAND's most common cause of AI project failure.[^2] Fix: write down the business number and its owner before anyone picks a tool.[^3]
Tools that don't fit the work: MIT found most pilots stall because tools don't learn from feedback or fit existing workflows.[^1] Fix: test on real cases, inside the real workflow.[^26]
Clean demo data that never meets your files: Gartner names poor data quality as a main reason AI trials get dropped.[^25][^2] Fix: run 50 real records in week one.
Trials with no end date: the average firm scrapped 46% of its AI trial projects before production.[^6] Fix: set a go-or-stop date before the pilot starts.[^4]
Budgets that stop at the pilot: Gartner expects at least half of generative AI projects to overrun through 2028.[^24] Fix: price the running costs, not just the build, before you say go.

Advice tied to one vendor: in an a16z survey, 37% of enterprise CIOs (chief information officers) ran five or more models, picked by use case.[^26] Fix: see two or three options tested on your own cases.
howToTest: Measure today first, so the after has a before.[^5]
Ask for a test on 20 to 50 of your own cases before you sign for a full build.[^26]
Agree the right answers with your own team first, and lock them, so the result is graded against your standard.[^26]
Ask for cost per correct answer, not the model's price per token (a chunk of text). In our document benchmark's hard round, one low-cost tool made 16 wrong answers; two pricier ones made none.[^16]
Price the lift: hours saved times loaded hourly cost, minus the cost to run it. Loaded cost is about pay divided by 0.685 for a full-time US private worker.[^21]
Ask why they picked their model: one maker's own list prices span about 40 times.[^28] In our benchmark, tools within 2 facts of each other cost from under 1 cent to about 30 cents a report.[^16]
Ask what happens when a better model ships next month. The price of the same AI performance falls 9 to 900 times a year, so a fixed system goes stale.[^27]
Ask for a client whose system has run in daily work for at least six months. MIT judged success six months after the pilot.[^1]
Ask where your files are stored, who can see them, and whether anyone trains AI models on them. Data privacy and security top firms' AI worries, at 38% each.[^6]
If AI touches decisions about people, such as hiring, lending or insurance, ask what documentation you get and who keeps it current.[^4]
Ask who clears unsure cases, how fast, and who covers when they're out.[^10]
Ask what they would tell you not to build. Google's first rule of machine learning: don't be afraid to launch without it.[^5]

faq.q: Is AI consulting worth it for a mid-sized company?
faq.a: Yes, if you bring one workflow with a number attached.[^3] In MIT's sample, partnered AI projects reached deployment about twice as often as internal builds.[^1] About a third of US firms with 100 to 249 staff already use AI.[^8]

faq.q: How much does AI consulting cost?
faq.a: On the US government's published price list, median hourly ceilings run $183.05 to $193.60 for AI roles and $164.37 to $166.89 for management consultants.[^29][^30][^31][^32] Those are caps, not prices paid; most consultants quote by project (30%) or by the hour (29%).[^32][^33] A lean in-house AI team of three costs about $630,000 a year with benefits, by our math.[^19][^18][^20][^21]

faq.q: Should we hire a consultant or build an in-house AI team?
faq.a: Hire or partner first, and build in-house only when AI is core to what you sell and you will run many systems.[^1] Most enterprise AI use cases, 76%, are now bought rather than built.[^15] Technical roles take a median 75 days to fill, against 60 for business roles.[^23]

faq.q: How long until we see results?
faq.a: Weeks for a first decision, about a quarter for daily use. Our sprint runs a fixed 30 days.[^17] Mid-market top performers in MIT's sample went from pilot to full use in about 90 days.[^1]

faq.q: Will hiring AI help lead to job losses?
faq.a: Not at most firms: among US firms using AI, AI-related employment fell at only 2%, and 66% use AI only to help staff.[^7] Of small-business owners, 87% say AI augments their workforce.[^11]

pickElse: AI is your product and you will run many systems: hire in-house. Technical roles take a median 75 days to fill, so budget for that and the pay above.[^23]

A standard job that software already does, such as scheduling, ticket routing or invoice capture: buy the product and test it on your own files.[^26] Most enterprise AI use cases, 76%, are now bought.[^15]
Under about 50 staff or no budget yet: start with a free SBDC advisor, or an MEP center if you make things.[^13][^14]
Staff only need everyday help with writing and search: buy an approved tool and train people.[^11] Of knowledge workers who use AI, 78% already bring their own tools to work.[^12]

offer.heading: Not sure you need AI help? Get a free 30-minute diagnostic
offer.body: Free, before any paid work: 30 minutes on your first workflow. Bring one job and what it costs you today. You leave knowing whether to hire help, buy a tool or skip it.

reviews.notes: Got the three answers wanted up top: is it worth it, what you get, what it costs. The 'twice as often' bullet read as settled fact; it now says 'in MIT's sample', and the key-numbers row marks it self-reported. Owner of the go, change or stop call is named first in who stays in charge. No neutral fee survey exists, so the page sets outside help against the cost of an in-house team instead of quoting fees.

Tripped on SBDC, MEP and 'price per token'; all three are now spelled out on first use. Recipe step flows name a role on every line and read fine on a phone. The before-number bullet lists what to measure (volume, hours, errors, cost per item), which is the two-week job they would own.

Asked whether one site or team can go first; recipe 3 now goes live at one site or team before scaling, as NIST's MEP guidance advises. Wanted the margin view: added a check to price the lift as hours saved times loaded hourly cost, minus running costs, with the BLS loading factor.

Read as a plant manager. The process-owner bullet named only a finance-side role; now ops lead, plant manager, claims or service lead, so it reads for any function. Clear on what their team gives: two costliest jobs, today's numbers and agreed answers on 50 real cases. The augmentation line (66% of AI users only help staff) answers the team's first worry.

Wants the price and a reason to trust it: no neutral fee survey exists, so the FAQ sets outside help against a roughly $630,000 in-house team. Free routes (diagnostic, SBDC, MEP) are offered before any paid work. The offer promises an honest answer, including 'skip it'. No founder name, no rival firms.

sources.name: MIT NANDA, The GenAI Divide: State of AI in Business 2025 (Jul 2025)
sources.what: MIT no longer hosts the report (its link now opens the NANDA project page, checked 26 Nov 2026); copy hosted by MLQ.ai. Sample: 52 organizations interviewed, survey of 153 leaders, and 300+ public AI initiatives reviewed. $30-40 billion of enterprise GenAI investment; 95% of organizations are getting zero return; just 5% of integrated AI pilots extract millions in value. Task-specific tools: 60% of organizations evaluated them, 20% piloted, 5% reached production. Over 80% of organizations explored or piloted ChatGPT or Copilot, and nearly 40% report deployment. External partnerships with customized tools reached deployment about 67% of the time vs about 33% for internal builds: 2x as likely, twice the success rate. Only 40% of companies purchased an official LLM subscription; workers at over 90% of companies surveyed use personal AI tools for work. For mission-critical work, 90% of users prefer humans. Enterprises, defined as firms with over $100 million in annual revenue, lead in pilot count but report the lowest pilot-to-scale conversion. Read 26 Nov 2026.

sources.what: From 65 interviews. Most common root cause: leaders misunderstand or miscommunicate the problem, or optimize the wrong metric; then missing data, chasing new technology, weak infrastructure and problems too hard for AI. Advises committing to a problem for at least a year.

answers.walk-away: Good AI help should leave you with one chosen workflow, a before number, a pilot in daily use, a plan your team runs, and every file handed over.[^3][^5][^1][^4][^17]
answers.human-role: Your team keeps every decision: the COO calls go or stop, process owners set the right answers, and a named reviewer approves anything touching money or customers.[^4][^3][^10] Among US firms using AI, 66% use it only to help staff.[^7]
answers.recipes: AI help takes three shapes: a free first pass, a fixed-scope sprint to rank and spec the first bets, or advisory while your team or a vendor builds.[^13][^14][^17]
answers.what-goes-wrong: Most AI pilots stall because teams pick the wrong problem or metric, and the tools never learn from feedback or fit the real workflow.[^2][^1] Missing data sinks many more, and the average firm scraps 46% of its AI trials before production.[^2][^6]
answers.benchmark: Judge any AI advisor by making them measure today first, test on 20 to 50 of your own cases, and show cost per correct answer before you sign.[^5][^26][^16] Then ask for a client running six months or more, and who clears unsure cases.[^1][^10]
answers.something-else: Don't hire outside help when AI is your product, software already does the job, you lack budget, or staff only need everyday writing tools.[^15][^13][^11] Hire in-house, buy the product, use a free SBDC or MEP advisor, or buy an approved tool instead.[^15][^13][^14][^12]
